summary: Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic used as an adjunct to thiazide or other kaliuretic diuretics in congestive heart failure or hypertension to restore or maintain normal serum potassium. It has only weak diuretic and antihypertensive activity of its own and should rarely be used alone. The usual dose is one 5 mg tablet daily added to the kaliuretic diuretic, increased to 10 mg if needed (occasionally 15-20 mg with close electrolyte monitoring). Its main hazard is hyperkalemia, which can be fatal; this risk is high (about 10%) when used alone and is greater in renal impairment, diabetes and the elderly. It is contraindicated with elevated potassium, other potassium-conserving agents, potassium supplements, and significant renal impairment.
indications: Adjunctive therapy with thiazide or other kaliuretic diuretics in congestive heart failure or hypertension to help restore normal serum potassium in patients who develop hypokalemia
Prevention of hypokalemia in patients at particular risk if it were to develop, e.g. digitalized patients or those with significant cardiac arrhythmias

dosage.n: More than two 5 mg tablets daily are usually not needed
Only with careful, frequent electrolyte monitoring

dosage.n: Used alone only with careful titration and close electrolyte monitoring (about 10% hyperkalemia risk)

admin: Add to the usual dose of the kaliuretic diuretic rather than replacing it
Measure serum potassium before starting and frequently after initiation and during dose changes
Re-evaluate the need for amiloride once diuresis is achieved in heart failure
Do not combine with other potassium-conserving agents or potassium supplements/salt substitutes
Withhold or interrupt during any illness that may impair renal function
moa: Amiloride is a potassium-conserving (antikaliuretic) drug with weak natriuretic, diuretic and antihypertensive activity. It is not an aldosterone antagonist and acts even in the absence of aldosterone. It blocks epithelial sodium channels in the distal convoluted tubule, cortical collecting tubule and collecting duct, reducing sodium reabsorption. This decreases the net negative electrical potential of the tubular lumen, which in turn reduces secretion (and thus urinary loss) of both potassium and hydrogen ions. When combined with thiazide or loop diuretics, it also reduces the enhanced urinary magnesium loss those drugs cause. It has little effect on glomerular filtration rate or renal blood flow.

absolute: Potassium supplementation/potassium-containing salt substitutes (except severe refractory hypokalemia)
Anuria, acute or chronic renal insufficiency, diabetic nephropathy
relative: Diabetes mellitus (high hyperkalemia risk - withhold before glucose tolerance testing)
Renal functional impairment (BUN over 30 or creatinine over 1.5 mg/dL)
Severely ill patients with respiratory or metabolic acidosis
Cardiopulmonary disease or decompensated hepatic cirrhosis
monitor: Serum potassium (essential at initiation and dose changes)
ECG if hyperkalemia suspected (tall peaked T waves)

preg: Pregnancy Category B. Animal reproduction studies in rabbits and mice at 20-25 times the maximum human dose revealed no fetal harm, although the drug crosses the placenta in modest amounts. There are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women, so amiloride should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: Amiloride is excreted in rat milk at concentrations higher than in blood; it is not known whether it passes into human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a nursing infant, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or to discontinue the drug, considering its importance to the mother.
renal: Contraindicated in anuria, acute or chronic renal insufficiency and diabetic nephropathy, because impaired renal function markedly increases the risk of life-threatening hyperkalemia. Patients with lesser impairment (BUN over 30 or creatinine over 1.5 mg/dL) should receive the drug only with careful, frequent monitoring of potassium, creatinine and BUN.
hepatic: Amiloride is not metabolised by the liver but excreted unchanged by the kidneys, so accumulation is not anticipated in hepatic dysfunction. However, accumulation can occur if the hepatorenal syndrome develops, and electrolyte disturbances in decompensated cirrhosis warrant caution.

major: Other potassium-conserving diuretics (spironolactone, triamterene) - additive hyperkalemia (contraindicated)
Potassium supplements / potassium-containing salt substitutes - severe hyperkalemia (contraindicated except refractory hypokalemia)
ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists, ciclosporin, tacrolimus - increased hyperkalemia risk
moderate: Lithium - reduced renal clearance and risk of lithium toxicity (generally avoid with diuretics)
NSAIDs / indomethacin - reduced diuretic and antihypertensive effect and additive hyperkalemia and renal effects
interactions.food: Take with food; avoid potassium-rich foods and potassium-containing salt substitutes.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol; may potentiate orthostatic hypotension.
interactions.diagnostics: Withhold in diabetic patients before and during glucose tolerance testing because of hyperkalemia risk; monitor serum potassium and renal function.

serious: Life-threatening hyperkalemia with cardiac arrhythmia and conduction defects
rare: Increased intraocular pressure, tinnitus, visual disturbance
emergency: Symptomatic hyperkalemia (paresthesias, muscle weakness, flaccid paralysis, bradycardia, shock, peaked T waves/widened QRS)
Cardiac arrhythmia or cardiac arrest from severe hyperkalemia

monitoring: Serum potassium - before starting, soon after initiation, at every dose change and during intercurrent illness
ECG when hyperkalemia is suspected or potassium markedly elevated
counsel: Take this medicine with food, exactly as prescribed
Do not use salt substitutes or potassium supplements unless your doctor tells you to
Report muscle weakness, tingling, fatigue, slow heartbeat or confusion promptly - these can mean high potassium
Keep all blood-test appointments to check your potassium and kidney function
Tell your doctor if you become unwell with vomiting or diarrhea, or before any surgery or glucose test
pk: Diuretic effect usually begins within 2 hours of an oral dose
Peak effect on electrolyte excretion at 6-10 hours; peak plasma levels in 3-4 hours
Store at controlled room temperature, protect from light and moisture
pearls: Main hazard is hyperkalemia - can be fatal; about 10% risk when used alone, 1-2% when combined with a thiazide
Not an aldosterone antagonist - works even without aldosterone by blocking epithelial sodium channels
Should rarely be used alone; it is a weak diuretic compared with thiazides
Contraindicated with other potassium-conserving agents, potassium supplements and significant renal impairment
Higher hyperkalemia risk in renal impairment, diabetes, the elderly and with ACE inhibitors/ARBs
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your normal schedule - do not take a double dose.
overdose: Overdose causes hyperkalemia and dehydration/electrolyte imbalance. There is no specific antidote; discontinue the drug. If serum potassium exceeds 6.5 mEq/L, give intravenous sodium bicarbonate or glucose with rapid-acting insulin, and a cation-exchange resin (sodium polystyrene sulfonate) orally or by enema; persistent hyperkalemia may require dialysis. Induce emesis or lavage for recent ingestion and treat dehydration supportively.
